speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I declare I am a medical doctor in a public hospital, looking after cancer patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am also an advisor to the Healthcare Services Employees' Union (HSEU).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Chair, SG60 is a time to look back and look ahead, and the same applies for our healthcare system as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is time for us to reforge, remake new foundations and move forward with new foundations for the future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Right-siting, which means place of care, subsidy of care, access to care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If the care has to be in a hospital, there should be a medical reason, not because the subsidy and access to funding is tied to the hospital or to the specialist outpatient clinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there is room to do further and do even better as we remake our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One of my Clementi residents met up with me and my team.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: He is a husband looking after his wife who is ill.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: His wife is a young mother, with a lung infection, with tuberculosis and she just got out of the hospital.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As part of a treatment plan, she needs to go to a clinic every day to take her medicines under direct healthcare supervision in a healthcare setting.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But because his wife is ill and in a wheelchair, he has to push her in a wheelchair to the polyclinic every day for the daily medicines.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My resident is a dutiful and loyal husband.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, his job cannot be done remotely, so he quit his job to support his wife, quit his job so he could bring his wife in a wheelchair to the polyclinic each day for DOT, to take medicines that have to be given under healthcare supervision.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could there have been a way for my resident's wife to receive her medication at home?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could there have been a way for the system to support my resident's family better, so that the husband did not need to have to choose between keeping his job and making sure his wife got treatment every day?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could the treatment have been delivered in the home itself?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when we help the patient, it can help the caregiver, and if by saving the caregiver's job, it helps the family as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People are getting older with more complex medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Healthcare is advancing and with advances in care, the use of scans is more common nowadays.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can we make it easier to access patients' MediSave for such scans, which may be medically necessary?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This will help patients with chronic diseases who have to undergo certain types of scans and if we enhance access to outpatient MediSave for scans, it will help cancer patients as well, who often have to go for regular scans as part of their treatment plan and monitoring.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the old days, patients would go to a polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They would queue and wait to be seen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That had its own challenges, but in recent years, there has been digitalisation at polyclinics nationwide.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have older Clementi residents who share with me that, while this has brought modernisation, it has brought challenges for some of our older residents as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In particular, we must avoid the phenomenon of digital drop-off when we go digital with healthcare, digital drop-off when patients who previously had access to care no longer show up, not because their healthcare conditions have gone away, not because their problems have been solved, but because they find it too hard to navigate a digital system to secure access to healthcare, or even a healthcare appointment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One worry that my Clementi residents share about is how they have to go online to book an appointment at an offline consultation in the polyclinic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These are the bookings for the next day's consultation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, it means that the residents or the patient with the best digital access, fastest fingers, sharpest eyes, quickest with their smartphone or their computer, they are the ones who "chope" the appointments.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The seniors who find it harder to navigate a website, find it harder to go online, they are stuck.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or sometimes, they are told to go and visit a nearby general practitioner (GP) clinic, even though this might cost more than the polyclinic, and for retirees without income, retirees of limited means, every extra dollar spent on healthcare is one more dollar drawn down from their retirement savings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH take a look at this again, as an interim measure, while the agencies continue working to improve polyclinic capacity and better support our healthcare sisters and brothers on the polyclinic healthcare front line.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, we know many seniors have multiple medical conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It comes with an ageing population, multiple doctors, multiple teams looking after the patients, sometimes the care is complex – many experts, many teams looking after the same patient – and so coordination is even more important today, and it is especially important when the care is complex.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I raised this 16 years ago, in the year 2009, in an article in the Singapore Medical Association newsletter, SMA News, and again more recently, in the 2022 MOH Budget debate Committee of Supply (COS).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Government, in the Cabinet, we have Coordinating Ministers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This can simplify the care journey, fewer visits to clinics, especially if the care can be coordinated backend.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means two or more specialist outpatient visits in a month.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine the impact on caregivers who do not have flexible working arrangements (FWAs), or who have loss of income when they accompany a patient, their loved one, for care.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, coordination is not just a cost centre or an expense, it is an investment, it is a catalyst, it is an enabler to help families with worries about caregiving.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we bring in social support agencies as well, so that more of the care can be done in the community, it can even be a pilot project for the Bureau of Service Simplification (BOSS), which I proposed during the Budget debate, and perhaps MOH and the Minister for Health can be part of this pioneering initiative to simplify the journey for citizens across healthcare, social care and citizen journeys.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, recognise patient navigation and coordination, not as a cost centre, but as an investment, an enabler and a catalyst.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The backend work of coordination takes time, energy bandwidth and our sisters and brothers in the HSEU have shared this as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, even as we invest in coordination, we have to recognise the hard work that healthcare frontliners put in to streamline care, coordinate care, wrap care around the patient.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we know from our sisters and brothers that sometimes this includes work taking place outside of duty hours and we should find ways to measure, recognise and factor this into our workforce planning.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also call upon MOH to look at healthcare information technology (IT), because when there is a gap between what the software is and what we want it to be, it is technical debt.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is AI being used to simplify the work for healthcare frontliners so that people can spend more time delivering care, caring for patients rather than navigating computer systems?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are we giving the same attention to IT that the big firms, like Apple and Google do?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I said in 2022, technology must serve the people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Technology must serve, adapt and bend to the person, not getting our people to bend to the technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And indeed, over the years I have spoken up for our healthcare workers, and in fact, as far back as 20 years ago in the SMA News, I and my fellow junior doctors had been advocating to improve the junior doctor journey, because our junior doctors are the future of our profession – and when we lift up, empower our juniors to do better, to be change agents – it lifts up the profession, it lifts up patients as well, it lifts up the care and quality of care in our community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On healthcare financing, I want to speak about support for patients and how financing decisions shape behaviour.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, just before National Day, I spoke in an Adjournment Motion on fertility preservation support for young cancer patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Every cancer patient goes through a difficult time, but for the very young patients, those who have yet to even start a family, it is especially stressful because certain treatments, while life-saving, can damage fertility, take away the dream of a family even before someone has a chance to start.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Working with a number of young healthcare workers across different hospitals, different clusters, we called upon MOH to look at four recommendations to help young cancer patients on the fertility journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If MOH moves on MediShield Life, this can be the first step to getting the Integrated Shield Plan insurers on board too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Fourth, support philanthropy in the fertility preservation for young cancer patients.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seven years ago, I spoke up in Parliament for children with rare diseases.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can MOH learn from this model, learn from this journey, to better support philanthropic efforts to help young cancer patients?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year, I spoke about access to insurance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I shared about young Singaporeans who are afraid to seek help in a mental health crisis because they are worried that once a diagnosis is on the record, some insurers will not cover them even for conditions unrelated to mental health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One Clementi resident said to me: "Dr Tan, some insurers are kind, but some are one kind", and indeed, we have to make sure that there is not such market failure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the same time, can MOH also improve access to non-clinical, more community-based mental health support, so that young Singaporeans with mental health worries can find help in the community without necessarily having to go to a healthcare setting.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If the situation is serious, they can go and see a clinical assessment, whether a psychologist or an informal medical consult, but at least there are more options there, even while MOH works out the issues with the insurance companies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: People must not bend to serve technology or the design of technology.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These principles apply not just in a budget, but across the whole-of-Government and in MOH as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I call upon MOH to consider our suggestions as we aim towards healthier, happier lives for the people of Singapore and our future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Thus, over an average month of four weeks, the total work hours should not exceed 320 hours.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Anecdotally, I hear that many junior doctors, particularly in our acute hospitals, regularly hitting or coming close to this limit.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For an average month, MOM's guidelines suggest that a typical work month would see one work 176 hours and even if one works overtime, one should not exceed 248 hours.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Why have we institutionalised the practice of overworking our junior doctors?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Employment Act does not mention that managers, executives, solicitors and such are also excluded from this guideline, and doctors, being highly qualified and with special knowledge, belong in this category.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To this I say, doctors hold the lives of the vulnerable and ill in their hands.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some indeed may be capable of operating at such an intense level for prolonged periods of time, but I believe many are not.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do we want our doctors that have been consistently overworked to attend to our sick parents and children in their hours of need?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Do we want doctors that are stressed to make decision that can literally involve life and death?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that in many parents' guides that MOH publishes, they emphasise the importance of parents being heavily involved in their children's life for children's health development.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many junior doctors in the public healthcare system are bonded and do not have the option of quitting if they are unable to deal with the stress and workload.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They have no recourse and are forced to make choices that compromise their family time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is it not ironic that even MOH, as MOH puts out these guidelines, their own doctors are unable to follow them due to the amount of hours they need to put into work?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the workload of junior doctors increases, many choose to leave the public healthcare system for better pay and lesser working hours.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This only serves to aggravate the workload of the remaining doctors, leading to a self-reinforcing cycle.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To me, MOH must intervene fast and decisively to change the system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Are the details of this recommendation and findings going to be made public?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Is MOH looking into more aggressively hiring junior doctors, especially those that have left the public healthcare system?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Will it include increasing doctor's salaries to better compete with the private sectors and, if so, how much?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Should we not strive to be a society that is kinder and more compassionate, especially to those that care for us?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget speech two years ago, I shared about how nurses' workloads are heavy, their shifts are long and they get little time to rest.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke up, calling for MOH to ensure that nurses have sufficient rest time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I ended that speech with a quote from a nurse, "We are called back for overtime when staff is down, when we don't go to work because we are tired, the management counts the number of times and mentions it in our appraisal for not being a team player and marks us down for it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We end up feeling burnt out and essentially hating the very job that we started loving.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: People leave because they see no end to this dark tunnel." I know there is light at the end of this dark tunnel and MOH has been doing a lot to address these issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share what steps have been taken to ensure that nurses have enough time to rest during their shifts and between their shifts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, what initiatives are currently in place to promote healthy ageing among seniors, particularly older women, ensuring they have access to resources and programmes that support their physical, mental and social well-being?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: How is the Ministry collaborating with other Government agencies and community organisations to create a comprehensive support system specifically for older women, ensuring they can age with dignity and security?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would like ask for the following updates.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, I am extremely grateful to MOH for approving two new Active Ageing Centres to be opened in Serangoon North Avenue 4, part of Jalan Kayu, after I spoke about the importance of scaling up Active Ageing Centres faster.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The public servants have responded to the Minister for Health's comment that he "was in a hurry" and "we are racing against time" in his reply to my Committee of Supply cut about this last year.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Four, Jalan Kayu residents are very supportive of the Health Promotion Board's (HPB's) healthy lifestyle activities.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With hypertension and high cholesterol having increasing prevalence rates among Singaporeans in the last few years, I would like to ask: one, how is MOH planning to extend Nutri-Grade labelling and advertising prohibition to key contributors of sodium and saturated fat in popular food and beverage places like hawker centres, food courts and restaurants in the especially high footfall city and heartland malls?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, what are healthier alternatives to sodium and how will MOH increase public education in this important health topic?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What types of cuisines that are popular among Singaporeans of all ages, for example, Chinese dishes, Indian food, Malay delicacies, Mediterranean diets, Japanese meals, Korean cuisines, just to name a few, have more developed recipes using healthier alternatives than sodium?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, will MOH consider increasing funding to: (a) Health Promotion Board to boost its "My Healthy Plate" initiative to now complement the Nutri-Grade mark for reduction of sodium and saturated fat intake of Singaporeans across all ages through developing healthier versions of recipes of our favourite cuisines and dishes that I have earlier described; and (b) will MOH invest in Singaporean researchers in developing healthier and affordable versions of specialty food additives that can make Singaporeans' favourite dishes still taste good but without the long-term harms and chronic diseases risks that sodium and saturated fat can lead to?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is to better support families with caregiving needs amidst shrinking family sizes and expand options for seniors to age in place in the community.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, will MOH consider sandboxing a new licensing and operating framework with interested private operators who are keen to innovate into more sustainable models for seniors with mild to moderate ageing needs, like how MOH did for telehealth?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What may be the timeline to do so and the selection criteria of private operators who are interested in participating?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With our ageing population, we can expect the demand for such services to keep increasing.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, how deliberate and how fast is MOH enabling the scaling of successful automation that can help augment the manpower, especially foreign manpower-intensive long-term care facilities, for a hope to blunt the cost increases when demands continue to rise?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Three, how many innovation projects for long-term senior care with some form of Government grants, whether it is under MOH or the National Research Foundation are there currently in Singapore and under the purview of which parts of MOH?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there any of them that are testing using frontier technology, like AI.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we look towards technological advancements to search for ways to blunt the cost increases of long-term care, we must not forget the wisdom of our forefathers in using traditional medicines to also deal with long-term chronic conditions and illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I have spoken since my 2023 Committee of Supply cut for MOH on the importance of understanding the efficacy of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM).

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very encouraged that MOH has since made progress in enhancing TCM practices in Singapore, including having the one-stop TCM Portal.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That means ensuring long-term care is accessible, high-quality and financially sustainable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have consistently championed this issue, raising it in Parliament through speeches and questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our entire ecosystem matters, from supporting caregivers and strengthening palliative care to enabling ageing in place through a robust network of community-based services, like Active Ageing Centres, day care, telehealth and remote monitoring.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The urgency grows as family sizes shrink and the cost of living rises, adding strain on sandwiched families struggling to care for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure long-term care remains affordable for all Singaporeans in the face of escalating medical costs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many will depend on Government subsidies, ElderShield, CareShield Life and personal savings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How frequently does MOH review these schemes to ensure they stay relevant as inflation and care needs evolve?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Cost efficiency is just as critical as affordability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What strategies are in place to reduce unnecessary spending?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Have we fully explored models like public-private partnerships or outcome-based funding to ease the financial burden on families and the system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Other ageing societies have implemented progressive co-payment systems to supplement insurance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could a tiered co-payment approach, where higher-income individuals contribute more while lower-income groups receive greater subsidies, create a more sustainable model?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Home modifications, assistive devices and caregiver support all add up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will MOH integrate these into a holistic financing model and framework?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there plans to expand MediSave coverage or introduce new financial tools to help Singaporeans prepare for ageing in place?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At its core, this is about fairness and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we striking the right balance between personal responsibility and Government support?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we rethink risk-pooling and cost-sharing across generations to ensure our system remains equitable and future-proof?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot afford to take a short-term view.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our long-term care financing model must not only meet today's needs but remain viable for future generations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to take bold, decisive steps to strengthen and future-proof our system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the last COS debate, I spoke about the need to improve home-based care for seniors with higher needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have also pushed for better support for their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Families are getting smaller, but the number of seniors needing care is rising.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Shared Stay-in Senior Care Services Sandbox is one such initiative offering a more affordable option.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I would like an update from MOH on its progress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I want to hear from caregivers and seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do they feel about the quality, affordability and accessibility of these services?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What support will be given to providers and how does this model fit into the larger strategy for long-term care and a broader ecosystem alongside home-based and centre-based options?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, what safeguards are in place to ensure good care and protect seniors' well-being?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How is MOH tracking and evaluating the programme's effectiveness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This sandbox is a promising step forward, but clear updates and a strong plan for the future are key to making it work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As our nation ages, we face two pressing challenges: a growing elderly population and rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: MediSave plays a critical role in healthcare financing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But do current withdrawal limits truly meet our seniors' needs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry aims to balance affordability with future needs, but are these limits keeping pace with actual expenses?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We live longer and face more age-related health conditions, requiring complex and costly treatments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we shift towards outpatient care to ease hospital congestion, outpatient medical costs invariably rise, putting significant financial pressure on individuals and families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this reflect adequacy or are seniors delaying essential treatments due to financial concerns?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this truly support a dignified quality of life for our most vulnerable?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry fears premature MediSave depletion if limits rise, but we must balance prudence with compassion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What good is saving for a rainy day if the storm has already arrived?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could a more flexible, needs-based approach be fairer?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could safeguards prevent fund depletion without denying relief?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could temporary fund depletion for essential treatments be allowed, with options to replenish accounts later?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore ages, our healthcare financing must evolve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we ensure no Singaporean forgoes necessary care due to financial constraints?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we make MediSave more sustainable and responsive to changing demographics and healthcare needs?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Chair, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs COS discussed three frontier technologies that will shape our foreign policy in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we got to get this frontier domain right and ensure that, well into the future, Singaporeans can continue to access and afford long-term care services of high quality.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To this end, I have a few questions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, could the Ministry set a clear policy goal for affordability of long-term care?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, we say no one will be denied appropriate services because they cannot afford it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But that is an assurance for Singaporeans with the least means.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is not a policy goal for affordability for the vast majority of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Today, we do have such policy goals for affordability for other domains of social support.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In housing, we peg affordability to various levels of income.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In retirement support, we crystallise the notion of adequacy in figures like the Basic and Full Retirement Sums.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For long-term care, what is our policy goal for affordability?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is about time we define such a goal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Also, when can we expect details of the higher subsidies for dialysis services to be announced?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Chair, last November, I asked the Minister for Health whether MediSave withdrawal limits can be adjusted every year, in line with inflation for healthcare costs, similar to the way the CPF Basic Retirement Sum and Full Retirement Sum are adjusted annually to take into account inflation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister replied that the MediSave withdrawal limits for co-payment of hospital bills are typically reviewed every three years while other MediSave features are reviewed periodically.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said, "This approach is favoured over automatic annual adjustments, to better account for other healthcare financing adjustments and enhancements that are continuously being implemented." However, I hope that the Minister can reconsider this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Automatic adjustments indexed to inflation would help many Singaporeans, especially the elderly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many elderly Singaporeans prefer to conserve their cash in retirement and pay for their healthcare needs using their MediSave savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is, after all, what they saved up for.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if MediSave withdrawal limits do not keep up with inflation in healthcare costs, then the elderly may be faced with escalating out-of-pocket healthcare expenditures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Automatic annual adjustments in line with inflation would only ensure that the real value of the MediSave withdrawal limits remain constant over time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government could still make additional adjustments based on changes in healthcare financing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to reconsider its position.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, many elderly Singaporeans find the withdrawal limit for outpatient care insufficient.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   I urge the Government to adjust MediSave withdrawal limits every year, in line with inflation of healthcare cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many elderly Singaporeans find the withdrawal limits for outpatient care insufficient.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should encourage people to seek outpatient treatment early before conditions deteriorate and hospitalisation becomes necessary.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, setting higher withdrawal limits for older Singaporeans is beneficial.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government can consider raising outpatient withdrawal limits and adjust them annually to keep up with healthcare cost inflation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans are not seeing their dentist regularly enough.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Over 50% of Singaporeans visit a dentist at least once a year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, 40% of these visits are for reactive treatment rather than preventive care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means many seek dental care only when they experience pain, often leading to more complex and costly procedures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am also concerned about tooth loss among seniors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Edentulism impacts the nutrition, social confidence and overall well-being of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How effective has this programme been in addressing dental health issues among older Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are there plans to expand or improve on it?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Oral health is an essential part of overall well-being.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, it is not included in the Healthier SG programme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Studies have shown that poor dental health is linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes complications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More public awareness efforts are also needed to ensure that all Singaporeans seek regular checkups instead of waiting for problems to arise.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Making dental care more affordable and accessible will improve the well-being of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This leaves many, especially our seniors, struggling to access timely and affordable dental care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will not only reduce waiting times but also ensure that more Singaporeans can receive the dental care they need.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Does Singapore have enough dentists to meet the increased demand?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If not, what is MOH's plan to grow the pool of dentists?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: During one of my Chinese New Year visits, I met an overseas dentistry student.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: She highlighted that unlike medical students, dental students do not receive pre-employment grants from MOH.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will help us build a strong pipeline of dental professionals to meet our nation's needs and ensure that every Singaporean has access to quality dental care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While we commend the Health Science Authority's (HSA's) efforts to curb vaping, it remains alarmingly widespread.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We can see people vaping on our streets, in smoking areas and even in schools.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: A key issue is the dangerous misconception that vaping is "cool" or less harmful than smoking.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us act decisively to protect our youth and public health.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) is widely accepted in Singapore, but remains outside our mainstream healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, TCM medical certificates (MCs) are not recognised by most employers, including the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is time to rethink TCM's role and take bold steps to integrate TCM more effectively in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This requires attracting and nurturing talent through scholarships, training programmes and career development opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The TCM Practitioners Board could require physicians to treat a minimum number of patients monthly and attend periodic refresher courses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This will keep them updated on advancements in TCM and maintain quality care.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thirdly, we should recognise senior TCM physicians for their expertise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: MOH and the TCM Practitioners Board could establish a framework to certify experienced practitioners, granting them higher status and potentially integrating them into the Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This recognition could pave the way for employers to accept MCs issued by these senior TCM physicians.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: By enhancing TCM's credibility and integration, we can boost public confidence and strengthen TCM's role in Singapore's healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us take these steps to ensure TCM is not just accepted but valued as a vital part of our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I was part of the second batch of psychology students at the National University of Singapore (NUS) when the programme started in 1986.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Since then, NUS has produced many esteemed psychologists who serve critical roles in MHA, MOH, the Ministry of Education (MOE), the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the private sector.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: During my time in the Singapore Police Force, I helped establish the Police Psychology Unit, which has since evolved into the Home Team Psychology Division, employing numerous psychologists.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Today, psychologists play a vital role in mental health – a field that is gaining increasing national attention.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, as in any profession, there are both competent and less competent practitioners.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Worse, platforms like Carousell are flooded with posts claiming to provide clinical psychological counselling, many of which may not be authentic, as widely reported in the press.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Let us act now to protect those in need and uphold the integrity of this very critical field.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms He Ting Ru, you can take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such professionals include psychologists, therapists and counsellors, the roles and work of whom many lay people struggle to grasp.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Concerns that the shortage of professionals will be exacerbated by introducing regulation have to be balanced against the real potential harm to already vulnerable clients seeking support from inadequately trained individuals purporting to provide therapy and the like.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just last week, worrying reports, emerged about unqualified individuals offering counselling services on platforms like Carousell.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Regulating this area also means that clients seeking help know that a professional has met a baseline level of training and understanding of the often-challenging ethical concerns that arise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also a first step for our existing financial health for healthcare financing to be used to expand access to such services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I, therefore, hope that the Ministry will develop a long-term plan to regulate the industry, taking into account the views of professional bodies while keeping an eye to make sure that barriers to entry are not overtly high.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A key part of this is to work with training providers and to increase the supply of qualified professionals to ensure that Singaporeans' mental health needs are adequately and safely met.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While access is important, the quality of mental healthcare services has to be ensured.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having real-time data about the efficacy of our mental health services allows both practitioners to recognise how they are performing and will inform the Government when developing a plan that includes standards on service quality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have two areas of clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Will the office also set minimum standards of quality across the services outlined under the tiered care model?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, can the data be readily made available in order for practitioners to use it to identify areas of strength, concern and ultimately, provide service quality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Cutting-edge research and development (R&D) in the medical and health sciences appears to show great promise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Of these, developments in precision medicine has shown up the potential to, in the words of the Singapore National precision medicine strategy, benefit groups and individuals through early detection, refined diagnosis and tailored treatment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have had announcements, such as the introduction of the Helix platform, to consolidate healthcare data and the SG100K initiative launched to log the blueprint of 100,000 participants through time, specifically, with the aim of understanding interactions of the genome within the Asian context.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are welcome, but one area that warrants attention is how gender affects health and illness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This goes beyond our obstetrics and gynaecological conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I brought this up in this House previously, how researchers now know that the same condition can present differently in men and women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a Time magazine article notes, women are not just smaller men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while progress has been made, there is still a long way to go.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would, thus, like to seek an update from the Minister about whether and how our efforts in personalised medicine will also cater to these gender gaps in medical research and treatment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, for precision medicine to fulfil its promise, it must go beyond collecting and analysing data to deliver real, tangible benefits to patients, and possibly even be used as tools to tackle concerns about ageing demographics and increasing care costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A data-driven approach is valuable, but it should serve as an enabler, not an end-point.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we move towards turning research into more effective treatments with fewer side effects, such as precision gene therapies, these treatments remain expensive, raising concerns about inaccessibility, which would only accelerate as the field advances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from increasing inclusivity in research, our health systems need to cater to the risks of inadvertently leading to greater disparities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would, thus, like to seek clarification from the Minister about the plans to ensure that advances in precision medicine translate into real benefits for those who need them most.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore has the potential to make great strides and lead in precision medicine.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But leadership is measured not by infrastructure alone, but participating in global research, increasing our ability to develop and test new treatments and most importantly, ensuring that the accessibility of these advancements are available to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to move beyond data collection to implementation, working to make the promise of precision medicine a reality for patients.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Wan Rizal, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my first Adjournment Motion in 2020, I introduced the LAST framework: Literacy, Accessibility, Screening and Time-out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad that these four areas are continually addressed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Awareness has grown and more people recognise the importance of mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, many who know still hesitate to seek help when they need it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They worry about stigma, who to see or whether their struggles are serious enough to warrant an intervention.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we need to strengthen our mental health ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One that is accessible, professional and safe; one that help seekers not struggle with long wait-times or uncertainty about who and where to go to.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With this in mind, I seek MOH's response on several key areas.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could more of these spaces be leveraged to provide timely, accessible support?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Another space to consider is, of course, the digital space, but such support must be human-led.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Oftentimes, I hear help-seekers saying they turn to recorded messages or AI chatbots.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MOH share its stance on this and what are we going to do moving forward?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could structured guidance be developed to support both parents and youths in navigating this process.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When youths are in crisis, they could end up in Emergency Departments, which are not the best environment for them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could we explore alternative crisis response spaces designed specifically for youths?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A growing demand for these services simply means that we need a well-trained workforce.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MOH provide updates on efforts to boost training capacity, particularly through the National Competency Framework and psychological first aid for frontline responders?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A workplace can either be a source of stress or pillar of support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some companies have made strikes in supporting employee well-being, but workplace mental health efforts must go beyond talks and campaigns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How can we embed mental health support more deeply into workplaces' policies, whether through structured accommodation, supervisor training or through pathways for employers for mental health-related absences?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could there be clear referral pathways to link religious organisations with professional mental health services?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What happens in childhood shapes lifelong health, including mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we must ensure that the right support structures are in place at home and in the community to help children thrive.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MOH provide updates on efforts to expand preventative health measures and nutritional support for children?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MOH provide an update on efforts to strengthen early intervention for children's mental health?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And how are Healthier SG initiatives being extended to support early childhood mental wellness?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unhealthy digital habits can impact mental well-being and physical health as well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How is MOH working to strengthen digital wellness efforts, particularly through resources, like the Parenting for Wellness Toolkit?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such efforts in mental, digital and physical well-being will ensure that every child grows up with the right foundation for lifelong health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I look forward to MOH's update on these critical areas.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Grow Well SG will work hand-in-hand with families, educators, healthcare professionals and community partners to create supportive environments where our children can thrive and sustain healthy living habits.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While the updated guidelines are very helpful, many families require practical tools to integrate good lifestyle habits, especially around digital usage, into busy routines.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I have two questions for the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: What is MOH’s target reach for the whole of 2025 for a start?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Second, can MOH share how Grow Well SG will be further reinforced with families, particularly in terms of practical resources and tools?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: And would these resources be made easily accessible for those who want to refer to them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Chairman, mental health is critical for a thriving society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: However, subsidised options often involve longer waits, while private therapy costs remains a barrier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: How can we ensure affordable support is readily available?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Community Outreach Team (CREST) teams play a vital role in early intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng
text: Tracking accessibility, early detection and long-term well-being is essential.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Keith Chua, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In his response to Project Hayat, the Minister for Health agrees we can do more in areas like research, the use of AI technology and means-restriction.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How will the National Mental Health Office work in the area of suicide prevention?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Will the National Mental Health Office take the lead in further policy-making across various Ministries and agencies, such as setting up a national suicide prevention framework?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Will the office consider going beyond the current framework centred on clinical services and mental health interventions outlined under the Tiered Care Model, and put in place systemic interventions targeted at suicide prevention?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For example, ensuring there is a holistic strategy addressing societal pressures and taking into account protective factors at each life stage from children to teenagers, to young adults and to the elderly?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, how will the Office ensure adequate postvention support for individuals and families, that is, care provided following a suicide attempt?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Countries with comprehensive postvention support, such as England and South Korea, find that the continuity of care for suicide survivors and those close to them are essential to preventing further suicide attempts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives are designed to help prevent the development of mental health conditions for all Singaporeans as part of the Tiered Care Model.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In the White Paper I mentioned earlier proposing a national strategy for suicide prevention, one key recommendation is to involve families and communities in such efforts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This includes strengthening collaborations with religious and community leaders, and the continuity of care for suicide survivors as well as families, friends and communities affected by suicide.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Ministry measure the efficacy of community mental health efforts, such as the Well-Being Circles and peer support circles?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Ministry ensure that every Singaporean has access to such community initiatives?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: And thirdly, Will the Ministry plan to leverage such community initiatives to ensure the continuity of care for suicide survivors and others affected by suicide?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But not many know about its mental health equivalent, Mental Health First Aid, which trains people to support those in distress or facing a mental health crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While there are increasingly more courses available online, access to Mental Health First Aid remains limited.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, we are familiar with apps that facilitate emergency first aid response.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, the myResponder app by the Singapore Civil Defence Force, with over 210,000 registered community first responders.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Their focus remains largely on physical health emergencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health emergencies can also happen anywhere and to anyone.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In those critical moments, the ability to respond quickly and appropriately is just as important.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, no widely recognised platform exists to guide people through a mental health crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is a missing piece in our response framework, but we do not need to start from scratch.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Integrating mental health first aid into existing emergency response apps is a practical solution with manifold benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health is health and this ensures it is treated as equally important as physical health.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A widely-used platform increases the availability of mental health resources, reaching even those who have never encountered or attended formal training.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: With step-by-step guidance readily available, users will be able to identify signs of distress and respond before a crisis escalates.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Just as we know to call 995 for medical emergencies, mental health helplines should be easily accessible through the app, to connect users to professional help immediately.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Collaboration with mental health organisations and other health apps can gradually expose more people to mental health first aid.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Social media campaigns can also help to promote this in creative ways.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, Tampines Fire Station has been making viral Instagram videos for a while now, and they are quite funny.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we could leverage on their expertise and do the same for mental health first aid.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, such apps need to be regularly updated with the latest information and resources to keep the platform fresh and relevant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Foreign mothers married to Singaporean fathers whose children will be Singaporean by birth, face significantly higher expenses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: PRs pay nearly $5,000, of which $410 must be paid in cash, and non-Residents pay nearly $12,000, with about $7,300 in cash.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many C-sections are unplanned emergencies, compounding financial stress.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given Singapore's low fertility rate, it seems counterproductive to impose such steep delivery fees on families whose children are Singaporeans from birth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, these costs send the wrong signals that Singaporean children are not welcome if their mothers are foreign.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This burden is heavier for citizen father, foreign mother families.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government's stance, as indicated in November, is that foreign spouses who do not qualify for PR can apply for LTVP or LTVP+, showing no defined pathway to permanent residency.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are all aware of the pressures that rising healthcare costs place on our families, the healthcare system and Government finances.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, let me say that we have done very well in achieving a high-quality healthcare system, one that is admired worldwide.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The 3Ms form the bedrock of the healthcare financing model, where which we have continued to evolve the system to deliver world-class care, without compromising affordability or sustainability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The roll out of Healthier SG is a key pillar.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Another key pillar is the shift to deliver more care at the community level – community hospitals, polyclinics and intermediate and long-term care facilities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Value-based care, integrated care models, technology and digital healthcare solutions and procurement reform efforts are also inflight to reduce costs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Enhancements to MediSave and MediShield Life, have also been made and will no doubt continue to be refined, to reduce the financial burden on both individuals and the Government.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While we have reason to hope that these efforts will help to bend the cost curve in the long run, it is also important to achieve costs efficiencies in the short term.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: What are we doing to ensure that healthcare remains accessible, affordable and sustainable for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The share of public healthcare versus private has been growing over the years, with the Government’s increased investments in healthcare.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Public healthcare institutions now provide a broader range of services, from primary care to highly specialised treatments and indeed, some of the top doctors in certain specialisations are found not in the private hospitals, but in our public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our public hospitals do also take in private patients.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, allowing public hospitals to take on private patients should not come at the expense of long waiting times for subsidised patients, which could in turn lead to pressure to build more hospitals, putting a strain on state coffers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Ancillary services too, something as simple as meals, must not drive up costs for the masses.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to monitor how public and private sectors impact overall healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, as we saw during COVID-19, and also with the integration of GPs in Healthier SG, greater collaboration between the public and private sector can help streamline patient care and make the best use of resources.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Healthy competition between the private and public sector also drives innovation and patient outcomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Does the Ministry have a view on the evolution of the public-private mix going forward?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And how will the Ministry ensure that both sectors work together to continue to provide accessible, affordable and sustainable healthcare for every Singaporean?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have made significant strides in how we address mental health in the last few years.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, there remain gaps in the level of attention, resources and recognition that mental health has received versus physical health, whether it is in terms of access to care, societal attitudes and in the way mental and physical health services are integrated.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have had many residents and mental health professionals tell me that even urgent cases can face delays in securing appointments.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And while MediSave and MediShield Life now help with hospitalisations and chronic diseases, outpatient mental health consultations and therapy sessions remain quite costly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Last year, we heard that the Government is expanding mental health services, including in the polyclinic and primary care setting, as well as in the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Government to expand and accelerate this further.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, the gap in the Healthier SG framework.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is needed if we are to promote a truly holistic well-being approach.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our GPs and family doctors need to be equipped to diagnose and manage common mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We should have mental health screenings in Healthier SG checks and more resources and incentives for mental wellness programmes in the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A related gap is the integration of mental health and physical health in integrated care teams.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Doctors, psychologists, social workers and allied health professionals must work together to provide holistic treatment for patients with both mental and physical health needs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Our physical healthcare system is truly world class, our mental health system must match that standard.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: What steps is the Government taking to close these gaps?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We all know the Government has given its commitment to keep healthcare costs affordable, as to make healthcare available to everyone.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It has rightly set up the three pillars of our healthcare financing system, namely, MediSave, MediShield and MediFund (3Ms).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, many Singaporeans are benefiting from the 3Ms.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: However, we still occasionally encounter residents who have sufficient MediSave, but are cash poor, lamenting why can they not be allowed to use more of their MediSave to pay for their medical bills.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Over the last few years, with advances in medical care, improvement in drug efficacy, higher staff costs, higher clinic rentals, these have all pushed up the healthcare costs in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We have moved from branded drugs to generic drugs, among others, to help to mitigate the costs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: While it appears to be in a stable trend, but it gives little comfort to Singaporeans, young and old alike.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are young employees who only after a hospitalisation, find that they have expanded their healthcare coverage for the year.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Their company had bought a policy is at the lower range because of high premiums.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: There are certainly lessons we can learn looking at other countries, such as in the UK's National Health Service, where the problems they are facing are somewhat similar up to a point – staff shortages, evolving healthcare needs, ageing population.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How can we learn from other's predicament and avoid getting into the same situation?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The 3Ms work well currently, but how can it meet our future needs?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Chairman, the most active exchange during this Budget debate has been over fiscal policies – saving as a nation or budget marksmanship, temporary vouchers versus structural support, increasing the Goods and Services Tax (GST) earlier or later.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Health Minister, I feel that I have a duty to somewhat weigh in.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Chairman, in the course of my speech, may I display a few slides on the LCD screens please?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When I first joined this Chamber 10 years ago, in 2015, the Government's annual health budget was about $9 billion.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I was then-Minister for Education; my Ministry was in second place, at $12 billion.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need the additional GST revenue, paid for mostly by those who are better off, foreigners and tourists, to continue to support universal and affordable healthcare for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The support given in healthcare is practically all structural, instead of vouchers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We can argue about the perfect timing for raising tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, if we do not raise the revenue in time while the population ages and healthcare expenditure escalates, we will not be debating budget marksmanship then.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There will not even be a balanced Budget target board to aim for, as our fiscal position will be deep in the red.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That said, we cannot let the healthcare expenditure curve escalate uncontrollably.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a bill all of us, ultimately, have to pay, as taxpayers, as patients or as insurance policy holders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But it is very difficult to rein in escalating healthcare expenditure, especially when it is a matter of life and death for ourselves or for our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Further, all round the world, people have high expectations of the public healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our three biggest wishes are for healthcare to be available when we need it, of high quality and affordable.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have spoken about these objectives in earlier COS speeches, but let me talk about our plans in the coming few years, for each of these objectives.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Hazel Poa asked about this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We therefore have the S+3Ms framework – Government Subsidies, MediShield Life, MediSave and MediFund – to cushion patients from healthcare cost increases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, seven in 10 patients in subsidised hospital wards pay nothing out-of-pocket, zero; while eight in 10 pay less than $100.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We constantly review and enhance the S+3Ms framework, to adapt to emerging clinical practices and also, new circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Last year, we updated the income thresholds to allow up to 1.1 million Singapore residents to qualify for higher subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A few months ago, we announced significant adjustments to MediShield Life, to better protect Singaporeans against major hospitalisation episodes, and then defray costly outpatient treatments like dialysis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most recently, we announced subsidies and MediSave withdrawals for vaccinations against Shingles.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Today, I will talk about further adjustments that we are making.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One, I start with MediSave withdrawal limits for outpatient scans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Over the years, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomograph (CT) scans have become more commonly used for diagnosis of certain conditions, such as cancer, as they are more detailed and accurate than X-rays.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A few Members of Parliament (MPs) have asked about this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This scheme provides seniors aged 60 and above the flexibility to use their MediSave for outpatient treatments at polyclinics, public Specialist Outpatient Clinics, as well as Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) clinics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This limit was last raised in 2021, from $200 to $300.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dental health is another area where affordability is becoming a concern.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Several MPs have raised this and asked if oral health can be part of Healthier SG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All of us remember in primary school, the dreaded moment the dental nurse comes in and calls your name, that was preventive care, long ago.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There has been a longstanding collaboration between the MOE schools and MOH to protect the teeth of the young.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Generally, a person needs at least 20 natural teeth to chew effectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Unfortunately, only about half of our older population have them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will take further steps, therefore, to encourage preventive oral care and hopefully, preserve more teeth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Currently, only Pioneer Generation, Merdeka Generation and CHAS Blue cardholders enjoy subsidies at private dental clinics for preventive procedures, such as scaling, polishing and filling.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will extend subsidies for these dental procedures to CHAS Orange cardholders.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I have met many residents, and these includes my own Citizens’ Consultative Committee Chairmen, who suffered from tooth decay and then decided to extract their tooth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I asked them, "Why don't you save the tooth?" It can be done via a root canal procedure, which is quite common now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This means the dentist will remove the decayed parts of the tooth, including the nerves in the roots of the tooth, and then fill it up, and then cap it with a protective artificial crown.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It adds to your 20 teeth; 20 teeth include those that you save.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They said no, because extraction was cheaper and it involves fewer trips to the dentist.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will have fewer and fewer teeth as we grow old if we take this approach.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next slide shows the net impact for a typical Merdeka Generation cardholder, someone with a tooth decay but decides to save it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For this senior, a molar root canal after subsidy costs about $700 at a CHAS clinic, that is the leftmost column, which he must pay by cash today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: After the subsidy enhancement, the out-of-pocket payment will be about halved, to $370.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He can also use up to $400 in Flexi-MediSave, so there may not be any cash payment required, and that is the rightmost column.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When subsidy goes up, we must prevent some providers from raising prices sharply and creaming off the subsidy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will, therefore, have to strengthen governance to prevent abuse, by introducing fee benchmarks for common dental procedures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Use of Flexi-MediSave will be effective sometime in the middle of 2026.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Prime Minister mentioned this in the Budget Statement, so let me elaborate.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Long-term care is for seniors who have become frail, disabled and dependent on others to carry out daily activities, such as eating, showering or changing.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are cared for in two main settings; one is nursing homes, or, at home, with support from community and home care services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan asked if there could be fee caps for these services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, both services today are heavily subsidised by the Government, with co-payment by users.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With an ageing population, our annual national long-term care operating expenditure has almost doubled over the last five years, from $1.7 billion to about $3 billion today, and it continues to rise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is because as one gets older, our care needs intensify.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is also considerable upward pressure on fees.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is mainly driven by manpower costs, especially post-COVID, where salaries of healthcare workers globally were reset to a much higher level.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To ensure affordability, MOH has been increasing funding to support nursing home providers, while also quietly imposing caps on fee increases for existing residents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We did not announce this but, quietly, we have been doing that to keep fees low.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, nursing home providers also absorb part of the higher costs for these existing residents.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for seniors newly admitted to nursing homes over roughly the past one year, they have been paying higher fees and this can be a financial burden to their families.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also not fair to the providers, most of which are charities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is time for us to improve our subsidy framework and significantly expand our structural support for seniors and their families.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The next slide illustrates the changes we are making.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The left side is nursing homes, the right chart is for home and community care subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The X-axis on each slide is the per capita household income bands, while the Y-axis is the subsidy percentages.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The white boxes show the current subsidy percentages, the blue and orange boxes are the additional subsidies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you see the leftmost two columns of each chart are now of the same height.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the maximum subsidy is now expanded to a larger group.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Provide additional subsidies of five to 15 percentage points, as indicated in orange, for those born in or before 1969 as seniors in these cohorts are not well covered by MediShield Life; and expand eligibility to cover from six in 10 today to about seven in 10 households, so more can benefit.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is more than a year from now.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, between now and then, we will provide interim rebates, which will keep the fees low for Singaporeans using long-term care services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Similar enhancements will apply to community dialysis services too.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will also increase the Home Caregiving Grant and expand the coverage of the Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund, as announced by the Prime Minister in the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The enhancements for these schemes will be implemented progressively from January 2026.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With these enhancements, over 80% of seniors, especially those being cared for at home, will pay less for their long-term care services.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Example one is a lower-income family supporting a moderately disabled grandpa receiving home and community care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2025, the interim rebates kick in, and their out-of-pocket payment will drop to about $500.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In 2026, when the full enhancements are implemented, it will drop to $200.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Thereafter, fees will continue to rise in tandem with inflation and income.
